deep.reconstruction:
CONTEXT. Page 17 treated the stereographic projection of the sphere. Page 18 turns to the case where the survey extends mainly along a meridian and is narrow east–west. For that case Gauss says 'Mercator's projection, taking the meridian as principal circle' is more suitable. This is the conformal transverse Mercator projection of the sphere (radius r).

Coordinates. x is measured along the central meridian from an origin of latitude P. The worked example shows x positive southward and y positive westward, as in Gauss's later Hanover system. Write v = y/r. Then y is r times the transverse Mercator (isometric) coordinate: if sigma is the great-circle distance from the central meridian, y = r ln tan(45° + sigma/2). Hence sinh v = tan sigma, tanh v = sin sigma, cosh v = sec sigma.

The foot-point latitude is phi1 = P − x/r. Consider the right spherical triangle formed by the pole N, the foot point F on the central meridian and the point Q:
- NF = 90° − phi1, FQ = sigma, NQ = 90° − psi;
- the angle at F is 90°, the angle at N is the longitude difference lambda;
- the angle at Q is 90° − gamma, where gamma is the meridian convergence. Lines x = const are images of great circles perpendicular to the central meridian.

I. Arc-to-chord ('Verbesserung der Richtungslinie') correction for the direction from (x,y) to (x',y'):
  delta = (x'−x)(y'+2y)/(6r²).
[Mine] The point scale is m = cosh(y/r) ≈ 1 + y²/2r². The projected geodesic has curvature ∂ln m/∂n ≈ y/r². Integrating along the chord with weight (1−t) gives (x'−x)/r² · ∫0^1 (1−t)(y + t(y'−y)) dt = (x'−x)(2y+y')/(6r²).

II. True (spherical) distance:
  s = sqrt{[(x'−x)² + (y'−y)²]·[1 − (y² + yy' + y'²)/(3r²)]}.
[Mine] s = d · mean(1/m) along the line ≈ d[1 − (y² + yy' + y'²)/(6r²)]. Squaring gives the factor 1 − (…)/(3r²). A further term, apparently +(x'…)²/(12rr), was struck out; it is of negligible higher order.

III. Geographic position from (x,y). These are series forms of exact right-triangle relations (Napier's rules), using sinh v ≈ v(1+v²/6), tanh v ≈ v(1−v²/3), tanh(v/2) ≈ (v/2)(1−v²/12):
(a) tan lambda = tan sigma / cos phi1 = sinh v / cos phi1 ≈ y(1 + y²/6r²) / (r cos(P − x/r)).
(b) tan gamma = tan phi1 · sin sigma = tanh v · tan phi1 ≈ (y/r)(1 − y²/3r²) tan(P − x/r).
(c) sin gamma = sin lambda · sin(P − x/r), exact.
(d) By Napier's analogy, tan ½(phi1 − psi) = tan(sigma/2) tan(gamma/2) = tanh(v/2) tan(gamma/2) ≈ ½(y/r)(1 − y²/12r²) tan ½ Conv. This gives the latitude psi.

IV. Inverse problem, from (lambda, psi) to y and gamma:
- sin sigma = sin lambda cos psi = tanh v, so v = artanh(s) ≈ s(1 + s²/3). Written as y = r sin lambda cos psi (1 + y²/3r²); the y/r first written was struck.
- sin gamma = sinh v · tan psi ≈ y(1 + y²/6r²) tan psi / r. Also sin gamma = sin lambda sin psi cosh v ≈ sin lambda sin psi (1 + y²/2r²).
- tan gamma = tan lambda sin psi, exact.

EXAMPLE. Triangle 3 of the French meridian survey: Watten, Cassel, Fiefs. Source: Delambre, Base du système métrique, I p.513, II p.800, III. Coordinates in toises from Dunkirk D:
- W (11819.0, 5593.9)
- C (13488.8, −4065.9)
- F (30442.8, 2107.6)

Log constants:
- log r = 6.5154903 and log r² = 13.0309806.
- 4.6855749 is the complement of log rho″ (log rho″ = 5.3144251).
- 0.7781512 = log 6.
- Their sum 8.4947067 (mod 10) = log(6r²/rho″), so corrections come out in arcseconds.

Plane bearings tan⁻¹(Δy/Δx), reckoned from south through west: DW 25°19′41.83″, DC 343°13′32.48″, WC 279°48′26.64″, WF 349°23′11.27″, CF 19°59′51.63″.

Direction corrections (log Δx − 8.49471, plus log(y'+2y)):
- WC +0.038″, CW +0.014″
- WF +0.793″, FW −0.585″
- CF −0.326″, FC −0.008″
- From triangle 1: DW +0.212, WD −0.423, DC −0.176, CD +0.351.

Plane angles from the bearings: W 69°34′44.63″, C 79°48′35.01″, F 30°36′40.36″, summing to exactly 180°. Angle corrections are differences of direction corrections:
- W = WF − WC = +0.755″
- C = CW − CF = +0.340″
- F = FC − FW = +0.577″
Their sum, 1.672″, equals the spherical excess of the triangle; this is the built-in check. The column −0.301 against each angle is not explained on the page. It may be a comparison with Delambre's reduced angles; interpretation unsure.
errors: CF correction: y'+2y = 2107.6 − 2·4065.9 = −6024.2, whose log is 3.77990, but 3.77833n (≈ 6002.3) is written. It looks like 2·4065.9 was taken as 8109.9. The effect is 0.001″ (−0.326 instead of −0.327); negligible.

The bearings WF (349°23′11.27″) and CF (19°59′51.63″) do not follow from the listed coordinate y_F = +2107.6. That value gives WF ≈ 349°23′50″ and CF ≈ 20°0′30″. Both written bearings are consistent with y_F ≈ +2104.0, while the arc-to-chord corrections (logs 4.12370, 2.17406) use 2107.6. Either the coordinate or the bearings come from a different value or source, or the digit is misread. The corrections are unaffected to 0.001″.
No errors found in the projection formulas I–IV. All are correct series expansions (to the stated order) of exact spherical transverse-Mercator relations; (c) and the last formula of IV are exact.
The struck term in II, of order (x'−x)²/12r², was rightly abandoned.

results.what: Spherical conformal projection with the central meridian as 'equator' (Mercator projection with meridian as principal circle) for a north–south survey
results.modern_name: Transverse Mercator projection (spherical); Gauss conformal / Gauss–Krüger projection in the ellipsoidal case
results.usually_credited_to: J. H. Lambert (1772) for spherical transverse Mercator; Gauss (1820s, Hanover survey) for the ellipsoidal conformal version, published by Schreiber (1866) and Krüger (1912)

results.modern_name: Line scale-factor (grid-to-ground) reduction with mean of 1/k by Simpson-type averaging

results.what: Formulas for longitude, latitude and meridian convergence from grid coordinates and inverse, including tan½(phi1−psi) = tanh(v/2)·tan(gamma/2)
results.modern_name: Spherical transverse Mercator forward/inverse formulas and grid convergence (Napier's rules and analogies)

results.what: Numerical check on a French meridian-arc triangle: sum of direction corrections equals spherical excess (1.672″)
results.modern_name: Closure check: Σ(t−T) angle corrections = spherical excess

deep.surprise_reason: Gauss's use of the conformal transverse projection with the reductions in I–IV is well known, from his Hanover work and Werke IX. The spherical version here is standard. The only mildly notable point is the possibly early date (bundle labelled 1813, before the 1816–1825 work usually cited), with a test on Delambre's data.

checkable.asserts: sinh v ≈ v(1+v²/6), giving tan lambda = y(1+yy/6rr)/(r cos phi1); result is O(v**5)
tanh v ≈ v(1−v²/3), the convergence formula in III; result is O(v**5)
tanh(v/2) ≈ (v/2)(1−v²/12), the latitude formula in III; result is O(v**5)
y/r = artanh(sin lambda cos psi) ≈ s(1+s²/3), inverse problem IV; result is O(s**5)

Mean inverse scale along the line, the distance formula II; result 0

transcription_corrections: In III the formulas read 'tang' (not '\tang'); the last is tang ½(P − x/r − psi) = ½·(y/r)(1 − yy/12rr) tg ½ Conv.
The struck term at the end of II is roughly '+ (x'…)²/(12 rr)'; it is illegible but clearly deleted.
The constant 8.4947067 is log(6rr/rho″) mod 10: 13.0309806 + 4.6855749 (complement of log 206264.8) + 0.7781512 (log 6).
The WC/CW, WF/FW, CF/FC labels attach to the arcsecond corrections (+0.038, +0.014, +0.793, −0.585, −0.326, −0.008).
The y-coordinate of F reads +2107.6, but the bearings imply about +2104.0; this should be checked against the image.
